What are peptides?

A peptide is a short chain of amino acids, typically 2 to 50, linked by peptide bonds.1 More than 80 peptide drugs have been approved worldwide, with insulin counted as the first,2 while unapproved research peptides rest mainly on animal studies and scarce human safety data.3 These pages explain each compound with cited sources.

This page summarizes published sources for information only. It is not medical advice and does not tell anyone to use a product. Questions about your own health belong with a licensed clinician. For questions about an order or a product, contact us.

What a peptide is

A peptide is a chain of amino acids. The usual dividing line is length: a peptide typically has 2 to 50 amino acids joined by chemical links called peptide bonds, and a chain of 51 or more is called a polypeptide.1 The proteins made inside cells are built from one or more polypeptides.1

US drug rules draw the line in a different place. Under FDA's biologics regulations, a protein is any alpha amino acid polymer with a specific, defined sequence of more than 40 amino acids.4 So a 45-amino-acid chain can be a peptide in a biology glossary and a protein in FDA's rules.14

Therapeutic peptides usually have molecular weights of about 500 to 5,000 daltons, according to a 2022 review.2 Six compounds profiled on this site show the spread, from 3 amino acids to 43:

Compound Amino acids Molecular weight (g/mol)
KPV 35 342.436
GHK, the peptide in GHK-Cu 3 (glycine, histidine, lysine)7 340.38, or 402.92 as the 1:1 copper complex8
TB-500 711 889.08
BPC-157 159 1,419.56
CJC-1295 without DAC 2910 3,367.9510
Thymosin beta-4 4311 4,96312

Two related rows sit on opposite sides of FDA's 40-amino-acid line. TB-500 is a 7-amino-acid fragment (positions 17 to 23) of thymosin beta-4, while the full 43-amino-acid thymosin beta-4 is long enough to count as a protein under FDA's definition.411 The difference is more than a label: FDA states that TB-500 and thymosin beta-4 are not the same substance.11

Why most peptide drugs are injected

Peptides are easily broken down by digestive enzymes in the stomach and intestine, so most peptide drugs are given by injection, according to a 2022 narrative review.2 Once in the body, peptides also tend to have a short half-life and fast elimination.2 BPC-157 shows how short that window can be: after one intravenous dose, its half-life was 5.3 minutes in dogs and 15.2 minutes in rats.13

CJC-1295 with DAC shows how a change to the molecule can lengthen that window. It carries an added linker that binds albumin in the blood, and researchers suggested this binding accounts for its stability.10 In two placebo-controlled 2006 trials in healthy adults, its estimated half-life was 5.8 to 8.1 days.14 The version without DAC lacks that linker, and FDA says the DAC version's pharmacology cannot be extrapolated to it.10

Some peptide medicines can be swallowed: semaglutide is approved as daily tablets, sold as Rybelsus and Ozempic tablets, for adults with type 2 diabetes, and the label states the two tablet brands are not substitutable milligram for milligram.15

Peptide medicines, from insulin to the GLP-1 class

A 2022 review dates the first therapeutic peptide, insulin, to 1921.2 The same review counted more than 80 peptide drugs approved worldwide and more than 170 peptides in active clinical development.2 A 2021 review in Nature Reviews Drug Discovery also counted more than 80 peptide drugs on the market.16

GLP-1 receptor agonists, the class that includes semaglutide and tirzepatide medicines, work by mimicking GLP-1, a hormone in the intestines.17 FDA describes three effects: they stimulate insulin release, they lower blood sugar after a meal, and they slow food moving through the digestive tract, which can help a person feel full longer.17 FDA approved the first one, exenatide (Byetta), in 2005.17 Tirzepatide, the active ingredient in Mounjaro, acts on two receptors: its label calls it a GIP receptor and GLP-1 receptor agonist.18

The GLP-1 hub covers the class, and brand-name products such as Ozempic have profiles built from their FDA labels.

Approved, compounded and research-labeled

The same peptide can reach people through different channels, and each channel has passed different checks.

Approved medicines go through FDA's review for safety, effectiveness and quality before they are marketed.21 Unapproved versions skip that review, FDA says, and compounded drugs are not FDA approved.20 A prescriber sets the dose of an approved medicine within its label. The Mounjaro label, for example, starts at 2.5 mg once weekly and, if more blood sugar control is needed, raises the dose in 2.5 mg steps after at least 4 weeks on the current dose.18

Compounded drugs are made by state-licensed pharmacies under section 503A or by outsourcing facilities under section 503B, and FDA reminds compounders of legal restrictions on making copies of FDA-approved drugs.21

Research-labeled peptides carry wording such as "for research use only." In FDA regulations, that statement is the required label for in vitro diagnostic products (lab tests) in the laboratory research phase.22 The label does not settle how FDA treats a product: in an August 2026 warning letter, FDA said evidence from a seller's website showed that products labeled "for research use only" were intended as drugs for human use.29 The research peptides page explains what the label does and does not mean, how FDA judges a product's intended use, and what a certificate of analysis should show.

How strong the evidence is

Health sentences on these pages name their evidence level: an FDA label, a human trial (with its size), an observational study, an animal study (with the species) or a cell study. The gap between levels can be wide. When FDA reviewed reports of suicidal thoughts with GLP-1 drugs, it pooled 91 placebo-controlled trials with 107,910 patients and found no increased risk.19 For BPC-157, a 2025 systematic review found 36 eligible studies, and 35 of them were preclinical, with no clinical safety data.23 A 2026 systematic review of the human evidence found 3 small studies with 30 people in total, all of poor methodological quality, and rated the certainty of evidence very low.24

Reviews of unapproved peptides as a group reach a similar conclusion. A 2026 review in Sports Medicine found that peptides such as BPC-157 and TB-500 show tissue-repair benefits in animal models, but that rigorous human safety data are scarce and they carry potential for serious harm to patients.3

Where the facts come from

Supplier pages are used only for what a vial contains, never for a health claim. Each page lists its sources at the end, and the page on how we source and review our content explains the process.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between a peptide and a protein?

Mostly length. A peptide is usually a chain of 2 to 50 amino acids, a chain of 51 or more is a polypeptide, and proteins are built from one or more polypeptides.1 FDA's biologics rules use a lower cutoff: a defined chain of more than 40 amino acids counts as a protein.4 Thymosin beta-4, with 43 amino acids, sits above that line, while TB-500, a 7-amino-acid piece of it, sits well below.11

Why are peptides injected instead of taken as pills?

Digestive enzymes in the stomach and intestine break peptides down, so most peptide drugs are given by injection (2022 review).2 There are exceptions: semaglutide is FDA-approved as a daily tablet for type 2 diabetes.15 For research compounds the data are thin; BPC-157, for example, was not detected in blood plasma after enema dosing in two human studies.13

Are peptides FDA approved?

Some are. FDA approved the first GLP-1 receptor agonist, exenatide (Byetta), in 2005, and the class now includes semaglutide and tirzepatide medicines.17 Many peptides sold online are not approved for any use: FDA states that neither BPC-157 nor TB-500 is a component of any FDA-approved drug.911 Each profile on this site states the compound's regulatory status, with a source.

Are peptides banned in sport?

Many are. Under the 2026 WADA Prohibited List, BPC-157 is banned in class S0 (non-approved substances), and thymosin beta-4 and its derivatives, such as TB-500, in class S2; both classes apply at all times.26 From January 1, 2027, the list names peptides in general as prohibited substances in class S0, according to USADA.27 GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide and tirzepatide are not named on the 2026 list,26 and WADA said their status will stay unchanged for 2027 while it waits for more data on athletes.28
